facts.fact: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so overheating can starve fish of oxygen.
Cooler water holds more dissolved oxygen: about 7.4 mg/L at 90°F versus about 11.9 mg/L at 45°F.
In warmer water, fish and other organisms are more active and use oxygen faster.
Warm-water fish generally need about 5 mg/L of dissolved oxygen for good health. Levels below 2 mg/L stress fish and raise the risk of illness or death.
Dissolved oxygen is usually lowest just before dawn (4 to 6 am).
Most freshwater fish can usually handle about 30 °C for a few days, especially if the rise is gradual.
JBL says heat becomes dangerous to fish and plants only after several weeks at high levels, not a few days.
Critical temperatures vary by species. For example, neon tetras struggle before rams do.
Nitrifying bacteria work best at 25–30°C.
Gouramis, bettas and Amazonian fish from sluggish lowland waters regularly face the low 30s°C and are more heat-tolerant.
Cool-water species such as goldfish, goodeid livebearers and axolotls are the most at risk in hot weather.
Aquazone gives these ranges: Betta 24–30°C, Neon Tetra 20–26°C, Java fern and Anubias 22–28°C.
A Vietnamese plant site says Anubias tolerates about 30–32°C, Bucephalandra about 28–30°C and Vallisneria up to about 30°C.
The same site says Cryptocoryne wendtii and C. beckettii tolerate heat fairly well but are sensitive to sudden changes.
Heat often slows or stops aquarium plant growth.
Signs of overheating include gasping at the surface, rapid gill movement, lethargy, hanging near filter outlets, loss of appetite and erratic swimming.
Fish gulping air at the surface is a common sign of low dissolved oxygen before a fish kill.
Direct sunlight, nearby heating vents and heat-producing appliances such as ovens, dryers and gaming consoles can overheat a tank.
Lights, pumps and a closed cover can push tank water above room temperature, even when the room is at 28 °C.
A pump with a dirty impeller can reach about 40°C and add heat to the water.
Metal halide lights run hottest. Several T5 tubes in a closed hood can also overheat a tank. LEDs run cooler.
A heater stuck on can quickly become disastrous during a heatwave, so check it.
In stacked racks, heat rises, so the top and bottom tanks can differ by several degrees.
Measure the water temperature with a thermometer before acting.
If fish are suffering from low oxygen, the most important step is to turn on an aerator.
Add an air stone or angle the filter outlet to ripple the surface. This raises oxygen and increases evaporative cooling.
Turn off the aquarium lights to cut added heat. Plants can manage a day or two without light.
In an emergency, float a sealed frozen bottle in the tank, but only where there is good water flow.
A Vietnamese plant site suggests wrapping a frozen water bottle in a towel before using it for emergency cooling.
Do a small water change with cool, dechlorinated water, aiming to lower the tank by only a couple of degrees.
Do not lower the temperature by more than 5°C/9°F in 24 hours. Rapid changes can cause stress and whitespot.
A Vietnamese source advises lowering the temperature by no more than 3–4°C within 4 hours.
During a heatwave, keep water changes to 25%, the same as your usual amount.
Opening the cover allows evaporation that cools the water by about 1–2 °C.
Cutting lighting time by 50% lowers the temperature by about 1 °C.
Cross-flow cooling fans on the tank edge, angled at the surface, can cool by 2–4 °C.
A Vietnamese plant site recommends cutting lighting to about 6–8 hours a day in summer, possibly split into two periods.
Practical Fishkeeping says a fan across the surface cools the water only a little.
Insulating the back and sides, and the front in severe heat, with Styrofoam or reflective foil can drop the temperature by a few degrees.
When insulating, leave the top open for gas exchange.
A chiller is the most reliable way to cool a tank. It costs several hundred dollars to over $1,000, depending on tank size.
Chillers are very expensive and use a lot of electricity.
Shrimp in marine tanks do not tolerate rapid temperature rises.
Step 1: Close curtains or blinds and keep the tank out of direct sunlight.
Step 2: Switch off non-essential equipment such as underwater lights, substrate heaters and unneeded pumps.
Step 3: Remove the lid or use a mesh lid, and lower the water level a few inches so jumping fish cannot escape.
Step 4: Add surface agitation with an air stone or sponge filter.
Step 5: Aim a fan, such as a USB fan, at the water surface.
Step 6: Feed only a minimum to reduce oxygen demand and pollution.
Step 7: Top up evaporated water, using RO water if possible.
Step 8: If overheating keeps happening, install a chiller.
Use a digital thermometer with an alarm for high and low temperatures.
A digital thermometer with an external display and min/max readings is recommended.
A fan controller set to a target temperature turns the fans off once that temperature is reached.
Switch to LED lighting. Consider a sponge filter on an air pump instead of a powerful canister filter.
Keep cool-water fish in the bottom tanks of a rack.
Check and clean pump impellers so they do not add heat.
Add an airstone before storms, because low air pressure lowers oxygen.
In heat, reduce fertiliser and regularly check Fe, NO3, K and Mg.
An air pump with battery backup keeps aeration running.
Place the tank away from windows, direct sun and heat sources, or use a curtain or screen. Check the temperature daily.
Running the room air conditioner on automatic helps keep the room temperature stable.
For a Vietnamese summer, choose heat-tolerant plants such as Anubias, Bucephalandra, Vallisneria, Cryptocoryne, Crinum calamistratum and Echinodorus.
In summer, avoid growing cold-loving plants such as mosses.
In summer, add aeration or surface flow, especially at night.
Do not add ice cubes or cooling packs, or do cold water changes. They cause rapid, stressful temperature swings.
Water that is too cold and oxygen-rich can form gas bubbles in fish blood, causing embolisms.
A frozen bottle without good flow creates hot and cold zones that can shock fish.
Do not unplug or turn down the heater. If you forget to turn it back on, fish may get cold shock.
Do not use PC fans. They do not cover the surface, cannot be aimed, are unsuited to water and can cause electrical faults or injury if splashed.
Do not hang mains-powered fans over the tank.
Do not reduce surface movement during heat.
Opening lids without a mesh cover lets jumping fish escape.
Cooler water changes depend on cold tap water, which may not be cold on the hottest days.
A homemade chiller made from hose coiled in ice water performed poorly and needs close monitoring.
Pushing fridge-chilled cobbles into the substrate has minimal cooling effect.
Do not pour cold water straight into the tank.
Vietnamese shops sell clip-on cooling fans (quạt tản nhiệt / quạt làm mát bể cá) sized by tank length. One seller lists 1 fan for tanks under 40 cm and 2 fans for 40–60 cm.
A Vietnamese source gives 23–26°C as ideal for most planted tanks. It says under 29–30°C is acceptable in summer for healthy tropical fish and plants.
Vietnamese sources suggest weekly changes of 10–15% or 30–40% with slightly cooler water, done slowly.
Vietnamese sources describe chillers as the most thorough but costly option, mostly for high-end tanks.
Myth: all tropical fish handle heat. Practical Fishkeeping says many tropical fish do not tolerate summer heat waves.
Myth: dropping ice in the tank is a good fix. Aquarium Co-Op, JBL and Practical Fishkeeping all advise against it because it causes volatile temperature swings.
Low-oxygen sensitivity is species-specific. Most fish are distressed at 2–4 mg/L of dissolved oxygen, and deaths usually occur below 2 mg/L.
